title: Caches: keeping the answers you need again
dek: How a cache like Redis takes most reads off your database, the ways to read and write through one, and what happens on the day it comes back empty.

items: A cache keeps recent answers in memory, so a repeated read takes about a millisecond instead of a database query. Redis is the usual choice.
The hit rate decides everything: at 90% hits, only 1 read in 10 reaches the database.
Cache-aside is the default: the code checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and stores the answer with an expiry (TTL).
On writes, update the database and delete the cached copy. Write-back is faster but loses writes if the cache dies.
Plan for the cache being empty: after a restart every read goes to the database until it warms up. The database must survive that, or the cache must not restart empty.

body.cap: Cache-aside for one restaurant's menu. On a hit, Redis answers in about a millisecond and the database is not asked. On a miss, Redis returns nothing, the Order API reads the menu from the database and stores it with a 5-minute expiry (`EX 300`), so the next request is a hit. A menu change updates the database and deletes the key.

body.x: Most systems read far more than they write. When 5,000 people a second open restaurant menus and each request makes 4 queries, that is 20,000 queries a second, almost all reads of the same few thousand menus. That is far more than one mid-sized database should carry; in the Lab's numbers a db.m5.large handles about 2,500. With a cache in front answering 85% of the reads, about 3,000 a second reach the database.
Reads from memory are also fast: about a millisecond from Redis against 5 ms or more from the database, and far less when a query would have joined several tables.
The water bottle on your desk. It is one sip away, so you only walk to the kitchen when it is empty. Most of the time you never leave your chair.

body.name: Cache-aside
body.what: Your code asks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, then puts the answer in the cache with a TTL.
body.use: Almost everything. The cache only holds what has actually been asked for.
body.avoid: Cases where the very first request must be fast; it always misses.
body.ex: `GET menu:r42`; on a miss, read the menu from the database and `SET menu:r42 … EX 300`.
body.like: Checking your bag for a pen before walking to the stationery shop, and keeping the one you bought in the bag.
more: If the cache is down, the code can still read the database, which keeps the site up but sends the database every query. Decide on purpose whether that is what you want (see the restart section below).
Store what the screen needs, already shaped: one key holding the whole menu is better than 40 keys holding one item each.

body.name: Read-through
body.what: The code asks only the cache; on a miss the cache itself (or a library around it) loads from the database.
body.use: When one team wants caching to be invisible to the code, or with a managed cache built for one database (DynamoDB Accelerator).
body.avoid: Adding a new service just for this; a small helper around cache-aside does the same.
body.ex: A `getMenu(id)` helper inside Zotato's code hides the cache from the rest of the service.
body.like: A canteen counter that fetches from the kitchen when a dish runs out; you only ever talk to the counter.
more: The behaviour is the same as cache-aside; only where the loading code lives changes.

body.name: Write to the database, delete the key
body.what: Update the database, then delete the cached copy. The next read misses and loads the new value.
body.avoid: Keys read thousands of times a second; every delete sends a burst of misses (see stampedes below).
body.ex: A restaurant marks biryani sold out: Zotato updates the database and deletes `menu:r42`.
body.like: Crossing out a wrong number in your phone book instead of trying to remember the new one; you look it up fresh next time.
more: Delete instead of updating the cache. Two writers updating both the database and the cache can finish in different orders and leave the cache holding the older value. A delete can't be out of order.
Keep a TTL as a backstop anyway, so any value that slips through stale is corrected within minutes.

body.name: Write-through
body.what: Each write goes to the cache and the database before the caller gets an answer.
body.use: Data read right after it is written, where a miss would be costly.
body.avoid: Data written often and rarely read; you fill the cache with things nobody asks for.
body.ex: A rider's current location, written every few seconds and read by every tracking screen.
body.like: Updating the shop's notebook and the main ledger at the counter before handing over the bill.
more: Writes are a little slower (two systems), but nothing is lost if the cache crashes: the database already has everything.

body.name: Write-back
body.what: The cache accepts the write and answers at once; it passes writes to the database later, in batches.
body.use: Counters and metrics where losing a few seconds of updates is acceptable, like view counts.
body.avoid: Orders, payments, anything you cannot lose.
body.ex: Zotato counts menu views with write-back. Never orders.
body.like: A shopkeeper noting sales in a rough notebook and copying them into the ledger at night: quick, until the notebook is lost.
more: If the cache crashes, every write it has not yet passed on is gone. The Lab's "Don't lose an order" challenge shows exactly that.
It also hides how much write traffic the database really needs to handle, until the backlog grows faster than it drains.

body.x: How long to keep things, and what to throw out

items: TTL: how long a copy may live. Long enough to get hits, short enough that stale data doesn't matter. Menus: minutes. Prices during a sale: seconds. A city list: hours.
Add a little randomness to TTLs (300 seconds ± 30), so keys written together don't all expire together.

Memory is limited. When it is full the cache evicts something. For a cache, use least recently used (`allkeys-lru`) or least frequently used (`allkeys-lfu`). Some defaults refuse new writes instead, or only evict keys that have a TTL.
Size it so the data that is read often fits. Watch the hit rate and the eviction count; a falling hit rate with many evictions means the cache is too small.

body.x: The day the cache comes back empty

body.cap: Zotato's dinner rush: 12,000 queries a second, 90% cache hits. The database normally sees about 2,300, just under the 2,500 it can handle. At 8:15 the cache crashes and every query falls through to the database. At 8:25 the cache is back but empty, so the load drops only as it warms up. For about 20 minutes the database is asked for several times what it can do, and it fails too.

body.x: A cache that makes the database look comfortable is also hiding how much the database would need without it. Ways to survive the cold start:

items: Run the cache with a replica in another zone (ElastiCache Multi-AZ, Redis Sentinel). If the primary fails, the replica takes over in seconds with the data still there.
Don't fall back blindly: when the cache is down, serve a simpler page, fail some requests fast, or limit how many queries reach the database.
Warm the cache before sending traffic to it, by loading the most-read keys first.
Or size the database for the cold-cache load, if the cost is acceptable.

body.x: When a popular key expires, every request that misses it in that moment goes to the database at once: a cache stampede. Three fixes, often combined: let only one request rebuild the key (a short lock with `SET … NX`) while the others wait or get the old value; refresh popular keys a little before they expire; and add randomness to TTLs.

A hot key is one key read so often that the single cache node holding it is overloaded, such as the menu of the restaurant everyone orders from during a match. Keep a copy in each server's own memory for a few seconds, or read it from replicas.

body.label: Redis, Memcached and caches inside the server

body.x: Redis has data types beyond strings (hashes, sorted sets for leaderboards, counters), replicas with automatic failover, optional saving to disk, and Redis Cluster to split keys across nodes. Memcached is simpler: strings only, no replication, but multi-threaded and very fast. Most teams pick Redis (or Valkey, its open-source fork) because the extras are useful.
A cache inside each server's memory is faster still (no network) but every server has its own copy, so updates don't reach them all at once. Use it for small, rarely changing data, with short TTLs.

items: Stale data: a cached answer can be out of date for up to its TTL. Decide per kind of data what is acceptable.
Two copies of the truth: bugs in invalidation show users old prices or sold-out dishes.
Another system to run, size and monitor, and memory costs more than disk.
A false sense of capacity: the database must survive the cache being empty, or the cache must be built not to restart empty.
Add a cache when reads dominate, and say what you cache, the key and the TTL.
Do the maths: total reads × miss rate + writes = database load.
Say cache-aside with delete on write, and why not write-back for orders.
Mention what happens when the cache fails or restarts, and how the database survives it.
If one key is very popular, mention stampedes and hot keys.

body.x: 5,000 people a second open restaurant menus, 4 queries each. Even the Lab's biggest database tops out at 12,000 queries a second. Put a cache in front and keep it standing.
